title: Can Believers Fall Away?
lead: Can a person who truly believes in Christ lose salvation for good? The Bible gives both strong promises that God will keep his people and sharp warnings against turning away. Christian traditions weigh these differently, and they also differ on how sure a believer can be of salvation.

sections.h: Promises that God keeps his people
sections.b: Jesus says that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand or his Father's (John 10:27–29). Paul lists those God called, justified and glorified as one unbroken chain (Romans 8:30), and says nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love (Romans 8:38–39). He is sure that God, who began a good work, will finish it (Philippians 1:6). Jude ends by praising "the one who is able to guard you from tripping" (Jude 1:24). John says those who left the church "were not of us" (1 John 2:19), and he writes so that believers may know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13).
sections.refs: John 10:27–29; Romans 8:30–39; Philippians 1:6; Jude 1:24; 1 John 2:19; 1 John 5:13; John 6:37–40

sections.b: The Bible also warns believers against turning back. Hebrews says it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who once shared in the Holy Spirit and then fell away (Hebrews 6:4–6), and warns those who keep sinning on purpose after knowing the truth (Hebrews 10:26–29). Paul fears he might be disqualified (1 Corinthians 9:27), tells the Galatians who rely on the law that they have "fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4), and tells the Corinthians that anyone who thinks he stands should take care not to fall (1 Corinthians 10:12). Jude urges, "Keep yourselves in God's love" (Jude 1:21). In the Old Testament the Spirit of the LORD left King Saul (1 Samuel 16:14), and Ezekiel warns that a righteous person who turns to evil will die (Ezekiel 18:24).
sections.refs: Hebrews 6:4–6; Hebrews 10:26–29; 1 Corinthians 9:27; Galatians 5:4; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Jude 1:21; 1 Samuel 16:14; Ezekiel 18:24; 2 Peter 2:20–22

sections.b: Reformed churches teach the perseverance of the saints: those God has truly regenerated can never fully or finally fall away, though they may fall into serious sin for a time (Canons of Dort, Fifth Head; Westminster Confession 17). Most Baptists hold the same, often called eternal security, and a popular form says "once saved, always saved." On this view the warnings are God's means of keeping believers, or they describe people whose faith was never real. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost by mortal sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance. Orthodox Christians see salvation as a lifelong journey in which a person can turn away. Lutherans teach that believers can lose faith and salvation, and Methodists, Pentecostals and other Wesleyan and Arminian churches teach that true believers can fall away by turning from Christ, and can return.

A related question is assurance: can believers know they are saved? Reformed and Baptist confessions say believers can have a sure assurance, based on God's promises, the fruit of a changed life, and the witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), though a true believer may lack it for a time. Lutherans point the anxious to the promise given in baptism and the Lord's Supper. Wesley taught that the Spirit gives believers an inner witness that they are God's children. The Council of Trent taught that, apart from a special revelation, no one can know with the certainty of faith that he will persevere to the end, while urging firm hope in God's mercy. Orthodox writers also speak of hope rather than certainty about the final outcome.

common: Christians agree that anyone who turns back to God in repentance will be received.
uncommon: Some evangelicals in the Free Grace movement teach that a person who once believed is saved even if he later abandons the faith.
